title: Pride and the Platform
subtitle: The man who is praised for a living is being slowly poisoned by his own job, and the only question is whether he knows it.
group: The Inner Life of the Leader

sections.title: Praise Is the Plumber's Asbestos
sections.body:
Every trade has a thing that kills the people who work in it. The miner breathes coal. The roofer takes the sun. The pastor breathes praise, and praise is poison that tastes like bread.

Think about the actual structure of the job. You speak and people listen in silence. You finish and they line up to tell you it was good. They name their children after you, ask your opinion as though it were settled wisdom, defer to you in rooms where you are wrong. Week after week, year after year, a steady drip of regard aimed straight at the self. No other profession is built quite like this, with the applause so constant and so personal and so tied to the man rather than the work.

I have stood in the foyer and felt it go to my head in real time, the swelling, the warmth of being told I matter. It is pleasant. That is the danger. A poison you spit out cannot hurt you. The one that kills you is the one you reach for, and praise is the one every pastor reaches for, because we are men, and men starve for it, and the church serves it by the platter.

sections.title: How the Self Swells Without a Single Decision
sections.body:
No one decides to become proud. That is what makes it so hard to fight. There is no day you choose it. There is only the slow accumulation of a thousand un-resisted moments, until one day the man is unrecognizable to everyone but himself.

It works like this. You begin to need the praise. Then you begin to arrange your work to get it, choosing the sermon that will land over the one they need, the project that will be admired over the one that is faithful. Then you begin to resent the people who withhold it, the critic, the elder who is unimpressed, the member who left. Then you begin to believe your own press, to think the gift is you, to take credit God lent you and quietly file it under your own name.

Not one of those steps feels like pride. Each one feels like normal life. That is the genius of it. By the time the swelling is visible to others, it is invisible to you, because pride is the one disease whose chief symptom is the conviction that you do not have it. The proud man is always the last to know, and the pulpit is the most efficient machine ever built for keeping him in the dark.

sections.title: Disciplines That Keep the Self Small
sections.body:
Pride does not yield to a single act of humility. It yields, if at all, to a structure of habits that keep working when your guard is down. Build the structure now.

Serve somewhere you get no credit, regularly, on purpose. Clean something. Sit with someone who cannot follow your sermons and does not know you are a pastor. Do a hidden thing every week that no one will ever praise, not to feel humble, but to remind the self that it is not the center, that the kingdom runs on ten thousand unseen acts and yours is one small one.

Invite real criticism and do not punish it. Most pastors say they want feedback and then make the honest person pay for it, with a coldness, a defensiveness, a long memory. So people stop telling you the truth, and the proud man surrounds himself with a wall of flattery he built by punishing every breach in it. Keep one or two people who will tell you the hard thing, and when they do, thank them, and mean it, even while it stings.

Give the credit away out loud and in public. When the thing succeeds, name the others. Not falsely. Truly. The proud heart hoards credit the way the body hoards fat, and the discipline of handing it away, repeatedly, against the pull, keeps the self from growing past its proper size.

sections.title: I Am Writing This to Myself
sections.body:
I want to be plain that I am not writing down to a problem I have solved. I am writing across to a problem I share.

I have felt the cold note when another pastor was praised and I was not. I have shaped a sentence to land for the applause and called it preaching. I have resented the critic and protected the flatterer and told myself I was simply discerning who was trustworthy. The poison is in me. The platform feeds it in me every week, and the weeks I feel most secure about my humility are precisely the weeks I should be most afraid.

The proud man cannot diagnose himself, so he must be diagnosed by others and by the slow work of God, which often comes as failure, as the empty room, as the criticism that turns out to be true. When God loves a proud pastor, he frequently sends him something humiliating, and the pastor must learn to receive it as mercy rather than fight it as attack.

Do not pray for humility lightly. He answers that prayer, and the answer always costs more than you expected. But it is the only cure, and the alternative is a swelling that does not stop until it bursts, in public, taking the church down with it.

sections.title: What the Platform Cannot Give You
sections.body:
The platform can give you almost everything a man wants. Significance. Influence. A voice. The sense that your life counts. It can give you all of it, and it cannot give you the one thing you actually need, which is to be loved when you are nothing.

That is the test God keeps returning the proud man to. Strip the platform away, the gift, the title, the applause, and ask whether the man underneath is still glad to be alive, still glad to be a child of God, still able to worship from the back row where no one knows his name. If he is not, the platform has become his self, and the day it goes, the self goes with it.

So build a life that does not need the platform to stand. A marriage that knows the unimpressive you. A prayer life that happens in the dark. A few friends who would love you exactly the same if you were fired tomorrow. These are the things that hold a man up when the praise stops, and the praise will stop, because every platform empties in the end.

The swelling self does not survive that emptying. Only the small one does. Stay small while you still can choose it.
